Kintyre: The Peninsula That Time Forgot

The Kintyre Peninsula hangs like a long finger from Scotland's west coast, pointing towards Ireland across just 12 miles of the North Channel. At 30 miles long but rarely more than 8 miles wide, this slender strip of land is one of Scotland's most overlooked motorcycle destinations. Made famous by Paul McCartney's "Mull of Kintyre" — still one of the UK's best-selling singles — the peninsula offers empty roads, island views, whisky distilleries, and a genuine sense of remoteness that's hard to find this close to Glasgow.

Getting There

The journey to Kintyre is half the adventure. The A83 from Glasgow through Argyll is one of Scotland's finest roads, passing Loch Lomond and the dramatic Rest and Be Thankful pass before following the shore of Loch Fyne. At Tarbert, you arrive at the neck of Kintyre proper. Alternatively, take the CalMac ferry from Ardrossan to Brodick on Arran, cross the island, and catch the short ferry from Lochranza to Claonaig on Kintyre's east coast — a spectacular multi-modal approach.

Campbeltown and the South

Campbeltown is Kintyre's only town of any size and has undergone a remarkable revival. The whisky industry has returned — Springbank, Glen Scotia, and Glengyle distilleries all operate in the town, making it one of Scotland's whisky capitals. The harbour is attractive, there are good restaurants, and the town makes an excellent base for exploring the southern peninsula.

  • Springbank Distillery — One of Scotland's most traditional distilleries, everything done on-site
  • Glen Scotia — Small, atmospheric distillery with excellent tours
  • Campbeltown Picture House — Beautifully restored Art Deco cinema, still showing films
  • Davaar Island — Accessible at low tide, with a cave painting of the Crucifixion

The Mull of Kintyre

The Mull of Kintyre is the peninsula's southernmost point and one of Scotland's most atmospheric places. The narrow road from Campbeltown descends steeply to the lighthouse perched on cliffs above the North Channel. On a clear day, the coast of Northern Ireland is sharply visible. The lighthouse itself was built by the grandfather of Robert Louis Stevenson. The road down is steep with tight bends — exhilarating on two wheels but take care on the descent.

Kintyre is Scotland without the tour buses. The roads are quiet, the pace is gentle, and every bend reveals another sea view, another island silhouette, another reason to keep riding south.

The West Coast Road

The B842 along Kintyre's west coast is a magnificent motorcycle road. Single-track in places, it hugs the coastline with views across to Islay, Jura, and Gigha. The sunsets from this coast — looking west over the Atlantic — are among Scotland's finest. Machrihanish Bay has a vast sandy beach beloved by surfers. The village of Tayinloan is the departure point for the ferry to the Isle of Gigha, a tiny island paradise with sub-tropical gardens.

The East Coast

The B842 along the east coast (confusingly, the same road number continues) runs from Campbeltown north to Carradale, with views across Kilbrannan Sound to the Isle of Arran. Carradale is a pleasant village with a small harbour and sandy beach. The Network Carradale Heritage Centre tells the story of the local fishing industry.

Practical Information

Kintyre is a 3-hour ride from Glasgow via the A83. Fuel is available in Tarbert, Lochgilphead, and Campbeltown — fill up at each opportunity as there's nothing in between. Accommodation includes hotels in Campbeltown and Tarbert, B&Bs scattered throughout, and campsites at Machrihanish and Carradale. Mobile phone signal is patchy along both coasts. The climate is surprisingly mild thanks to the Gulf Stream — palm trees grow in several gardens. Best months: May to September. keyTakeaways: Kintyre is a slender 30-mile peninsula rarely more than 8 miles wide, offering empty roads and remoteness within three hours of Glasgow.
The A83 from Glasgow through Argyll is one of Scotland's finest approaches, passing Loch Lomond and the Rest and Be Thankful.
Campbeltown has revived as a whisky capital, with Springbank, Glen Scotia and Glengyle distilleries all operating in town.
The Mull of Kintyre gives views to Northern Ireland, reached by a steep, twisting descent to the lighthouse.
Fuel is only available in Tarbert, Lochgilphead and Campbeltown, so fill up at every opportunity.

faq.q: How do I get to the Kintyre Peninsula?
faq.a: Kintyre is a three-hour ride from Glasgow via the A83, one of Scotland's finest roads, passing Loch Lomond and the dramatic Rest and Be Thankful before following the shore of Loch Fyne. Alternatively, take the CalMac ferry from Ardrossan to Arran, cross the island, and catch the short ferry from Lochranza to Claonaig on Kintyre's east coast.

faq.q: Is Campbeltown a good whisky destination?
faq.a: Yes. Campbeltown has undergone a remarkable revival and is now one of Scotland's whisky capitals, with Springbank, Glen Scotia and Glengyle distilleries all operating in the town. Springbank is one of Scotland's most traditional distilleries, doing everything on-site, while Glen Scotia offers atmospheric small-scale tours.

faq.q: What is the ride to the Mull of Kintyre like?
faq.a: The narrow road from Campbeltown descends steeply to the lighthouse perched on cliffs above the North Channel, and on a clear day the coast of Northern Ireland is sharply visible. The descent is steep with tight bends, so it is exhilarating on two wheels but demands care. The lighthouse was built by Robert Louis Stevenson's grandfather.

faq.q: Where can I refuel on Kintyre?
faq.a: Fuel is available in Tarbert, Lochgilphead and Campbeltown, so fill up at each opportunity as there is nothing in between. Mobile phone signal is also patchy along both coasts, so plan ahead. The climate is surprisingly mild thanks to the Gulf Stream, and palm trees grow in several gardens.

faq.q: How long should I spend on Kintyre?
faq.a: Allow at least two days to do the peninsula justice, and three if you want to include the Isle of Gigha (ferry from Tayinloan) or take a distillery tour. The best months are May to September. Accommodation includes hotels in Campbeltown and Tarbert, scattered B&Bs, and campsites at Machrihanish and Carradale.
